The airport is owned by the City of McKinney and is home to many business aircraft and fleets for global companies, like Texas Instruments and Toyota Motor Corporation.

    In 2025, the city approved the construction of the newly introduced commercial passenger terminal for $72 million. This has now lured in Avelo as the first operator at the airport. Avelo remains the only airline to announce flights from the airport, with hometown Dallas airline Southwest already signaling it has no immediate interest in serving the airport as the 'numbers don't stack up'.

    On November 19, McKinney gained two more nonstop domestic flights from Avelo, as Fort Lauderdale and Tampa began regular scheduled services. The airline will operate the route to Fort Lauderdale up to six times weekly, while Tampa sees a four-weekly rotation.

    According to recent reports, additional flights are set to begin in December, with Atlanta, Denver, and Sarasota scheduled to all commence on December 16. This will be the airline's biggest one-day expansion from McKinney, with three new services all beginning on the same day.

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting mentioned the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    It has been revealed that “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the latest people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she mentioned.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday stated at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he stated. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., noted Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the newly introduced ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve remarked many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who stated he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    Recent findings suggest that “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he stated. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    In a recent development, “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he noted. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but stated, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    According to recent reports, “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    Industry observers note that “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    In a recent development, “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he remarked. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., mentioned, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short.
    • At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft.
    • Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

    At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story….

    Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

    The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only indicated as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

    It has been revealed that there was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

    After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

    Recent findings suggest that but anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

    As I remarked above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

    We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

    If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

    Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

    It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

    Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia.
    • Hyatt has declared looks for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland.
    • The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

    Hyatt has declared looks for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

    The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

    Sources indicate that there are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

    Industry observers note that while a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

    Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:.

    “The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”.

    There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

    This will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

    In a recent development, world of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

    First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:.

    According to recent reports, the area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

    It has been revealed that I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any….

    According to recent reports, the Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

    It’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

    What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane?

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
    • It has been revealed that former Rep.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    It has been revealed that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

    According to recent reports, the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    According to recent reports, peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    It has been revealed that but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Newly introduced York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has mentioned she had no connection to the scheme.

    Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    Recent findings suggest that the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    In a recent development, "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    Sources indicate that the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1345 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….
    • When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.
    • It has been revealed that in general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….

    When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

    It has been revealed that in general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”.

    Meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a tech giant identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”.

    In some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:.

    While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order….

    In a recent development, aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

    British Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

    According to recent reports, while this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

    Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the company’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”.

    For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

    In a recent development, PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

    The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

    For those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

    China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

    So, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

    According to recent reports, starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

    In a recent development, the reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the organization’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

    Industry observers note that south African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

    Recent findings suggest that atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a major operation.

    According to recent reports, the callsign is presumably a reflection of the organization’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

    According to recent reports, kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

    European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

    Airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

    What’s your favorite airline callsign?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    2 Virgin Australia Pilots Admit They’re Too Tired To Continue Flying, Immediately Offloaded

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that two Virgin Australia pilots declared themselves unfit to continue flying after fatigue set in during a domestic flight from Melbourne Airport (MEL) to Adelaide Airport (ADL) on Wednesday.
    • In a recent development, the incident highlights the importance of fatigue management in commercial aviation, where pilots must recognize when tiredness could compromise their ability to operate an aircraft safely.
    • According to AIRLIVE, the incident occurred aboard VA219 on Wednesday morning.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that two Virgin Australia pilots declared themselves unfit to continue flying after fatigue set in during a domestic flight from Melbourne Airport (MEL) to Adelaide Airport (ADL) on Wednesday. Both crew members requested to be stood down upon reaching their destination. The aircraft landed safely at Adelaide Airport, after which the pilots were immediately removed from further flying duties.

    In a recent development, the incident highlights the importance of fatigue management in commercial aviation, where pilots must recognize when tiredness could compromise their ability to operate an aircraft safely. Although the flight itself was completed without incident, the decision to remove both pilots raises broader questions about crew scheduling, rest periods, and the challenges of managing fatigue across Australia's airline industry. Virgin Australia's response also shows why self-reporting remains essential to aviation safety.

    According to AIRLIVE, the incident occurred aboard VA219 on Wednesday morning. The Boeing 737-800, registered VH-VUX, was operating a domestic service between Melbourne and Adelaide when both pilots reported fatigue. Rather than continue their planned duties, the flight crew requested to be stood down at their next destination.

    Sources indicate that the aircraft continued to Adelaide and completed its journey safely, touching down at 11:05 local time. The flight had departed Melbourne about an hour earlier, following the aircraft's previous operation of flight VA814 from Sydney to Melbourne earlier that morning. Once in Adelaide, both pilots were immediately offloaded, preventing them from operating any subsequent flight sectors until they were considered fit to return to duty.

    In a recent development, the decision followed Virgin Australia's fatigue risk management procedures, which allow pilots to report when tiredness affects their ability to perform their responsibilities safely. Importantly, declaring oneself unfit to fly is not an admission of wrongdoing. It is a safety measure designed to prevent potentially impaired crew members from continuing operations.

    This is not the first time fatigue management has attracted attention at Virgin Australia. In May 2024, The Guardian reported that senior pilots had raised concerns about the airline's rostering arrangements, arguing that demanding schedules were contributing to fatigue across the pilot workforce. Correspondence reviewed by the newspaper highlighted concerns about consecutive long duty days, sometimes lasting 11–12 hours, followed by the minimum 12-hour rest period permitted under the applicable rules.

    The pilots also questioned the airline's rostering software and its ability to accommodate operational realities, particularly when flights were delayed. Virgin Australia responded at the time by saying it operated under a robust fatigue management system approved by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). The airline also highlighted that its pilots received 156 rostered days off annually. Although those earlier concerns do not establish the cause of the November 2026 report, they illustrate how crew scheduling and fatigue have remained crucial topics within the airline.

    Fatigue is also a concern beyond the flight deck. Last month, ABC News reported on an Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation into a taxiway incident at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) involving Virgin Australia flight 1589 and Qantas flight 420. An air traffic controller working during the incident had a high predicted fatigue risk after being rostered to finish at 8:50 PM and return to duty at 5:30 AM the following morning. The ATSB stressed that a high predicted fatigue level does not necessarily mean an individual is actually fatigued. Nevertheless, the case demonstrates how demanding schedules can affect safety-critical aviation personnel across different operational environments.

    According to recent reports, fatigue can significantly affect a pilot's concentration, reaction time, memory, and decision-making under pressure. According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), tiredness can reduce the ability to perform tasks requiring manual coordination, vigilance, and higher-level cognitive processing. These effects can develop after a single demanding period or accumulate over several days of insufficient rest.

    The consequences can be particularly serious in commercial aviation, where pilots must continuously monitor aircraft systems, communicate with air traffic control, assess changing weather conditions, and respond to unexpected situations. Even experienced flight crew members are not immune to these effects. The FAA also notes that coffee, medication, motivation, and willpower cannot overcome fatigue; adequate sleep remains the most effective solution.

    In a recent development, virgin Australia's decision to remove both pilots from further duties should be viewed positively. Allowing fatigued crew members to keep flying just to avoid disruption would create an unnecessary safety risk for passengers, other crew members, and everyone involved in the operation. While replacing pilots can create scheduling complications and potentially delay subsequent services, those considerations must remain secondary to operational safety.

    In a recent development, this incident demonstrates an important principle of commercial aviation: a flight is only safe when its crew members are fit to perform their duties. By allowing both pilots to report their condition and immediately standing them down after arrival, Virgin Australia followed the appropriate safety-first approach.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

    LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the newly introduced long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

    It has been revealed that the airline intends to use these planes to open up new long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”.

    Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been unveiled.

    Industry observers note that we can expect LATAM to offer an all-upcoming passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:.

    Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV reveals. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

    According to recent reports, LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

    It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

    It has been revealed that LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

    Recent findings suggest that the A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

    LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

    For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

    It has been revealed that while American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

    Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being remarked, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”.

    While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

    To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

    In a recent development, in early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline plans to use to grow into newly introduced markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

    Industry observers note that ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is at the moment offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

    LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two latest wide body business class products over the past several years.

    What do you make of LATAM’s new A321XLR business class?

    #31010. Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2928 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026.
    • It has been revealed that however, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee.
    • This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

    It has been revealed that however, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

    This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

    Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card.

    Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:.

    Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:.

    With the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited currently has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

    Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

    Admittedly the spending requirement is substantial (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

    If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

    Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

    Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

    In a recent development, when it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

    With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

    According to recent reports, in fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

    No Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history.

    It has been revealed that in terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:.

    All cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like that.

    2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

    Meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

    American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

    This program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

    Recent findings suggest that you can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

    In a recent development, personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

    Sources indicate that it’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

    Sources indicate that I think the glitch is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back. It’s just not a latest concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

    So who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:.

    I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

    Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

    Sources indicate that perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

    The upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

    It has been revealed that another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

    According to recent reports, if you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

    Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

    As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

    While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

    The card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

    I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

    I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

    In addition to a big welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer. The card also offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

    Ultimately I’d consider this to be a niche card. The card could be worth getting for the excellent welcome offer, and it could be worth it if you have a business that spends a huge amount, and values the lack of a preset spending limit, the card’s Amex branding, and/or the statement credits.

    Beyond that, though, I tend to think there are better options. If you’re not a huge spender, the Amex Blue Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Plus are excellent options. If you’re willing to maximize points and bonus categories, consider the Amex Business Gold. And if you’re looking for the best direct alternative that’s arguably more lucrative, consider the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

    #31009. Industry News: Flexibility: How Flight Attendants Can Be Displaced From Their Schedule With Little Notice

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1639 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Flexibility: How Flight Attendants Can Be Displaced From Their Schedule With Little Notice

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Flight attendants' schedules in the US can change at short notice in several ways, but union contracts set limits on how it happens and what they're paid when it does.
    • Sources indicate that in the rest of the world, it's a little bit different, and unions rarely have much input.
    • When a trip or part of a trip is canceled, crew scheduling can move the affected flight attendant to another trip, put them on reserve/standby, or release them from duty entirely.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Flight attendants' schedules in the US can change at short notice in several ways, but union contracts set limits on how it happens and what they're paid when it does. This guide will take a closer look at how it all works, when things change at the last minute, and what can happen to a flight attendant's schedule.

    Sources indicate that in the rest of the world, it's a little bit different, and unions rarely have much input. It's all down to the airlines' operations teams and aviation regulators when it comes to how our schedules can change. Of course, flexibility is key, and things can happen unexpectedly, but that's all part of the fun of being a flight attendant or cabin crew.

    When a trip or part of a trip is canceled, crew scheduling can move the affected flight attendant to another trip, put them on reserve/standby, or release them from duty entirely. One older contract, filed with the SEC, pays them for whichever is greater: the original assignment or the new one. Many US airline contracts call this "pay protection." This is a contractual rule that keeps a flight attendant's scheduled pay credit safe when flights change, get canceled, or get delayed through no fault of their own.

    Industry observers note that if the trip or a leg of the sequence is canceled, union collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) typically guarantee that they still get paid for the original scheduled value or the newly introduced assigned trip, whichever is greater. If crew scheduling alters the route or equipment after a disruption, pay protection ensures that they do not lose money if the new assignment ends up paying less than what was originally on the line.

    Alaska Airlines' current agreement, for example, can remove a flight attendant from an assignment with pay protection and fly them home as a passenger; this is called deadheading. Under the 2025-2028 Collective Bargaining Agreement between Alaska Airlines and the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, line-holding flight attendants receive 150% pay on top of strong base trip protection when crew scheduling reassigns or reroutes a sequence. If a crew member is assigned to four or more legs over the original sequence, pay is 200%.

    Trip displacement occurs when a crew member is involuntarily removed from a scheduled flight pairing or stranded away from their planned itinerary. This could be due to operational needs, regulatory limits, or personnel bumps; it is not a personal absence from duty. It can vary from airline to airline in the US, and union contracts may vary. At carriers without union contracts, such as Delta Air Lines, displaced flight attendants often do not receive automatic pay protection and must choose between sitting on-call availability or taking a lesser payment.

    Recent findings suggest that A flight attendant can also be bumped from a trip that they bid for. They can be displaced from trips to make room for training or for upcoming hires' supervised flights, which are called operating experience. A flight attendant can be pulled from a trip so a supervisor, for example, can occupy that position for qualification or observation. In those cases, the displaced flight attendant gets a similar trip or is released from duty for the rest of the trip.

    Frontier Airlines' 2019 contract requires at least 24 hours' notice before a flight attendant is displaced, and pays them for the trip they lost. Depending on the contract, crew scheduling may have a specific window (often matching the original trip's footprint) to assign replacement flights. If the airline does not reassign the flight attendant within those rules, the crew member is released with pay.

    The one thing that most often catches US flight attendants off guard is the junior assignment, sometimes called junior availability or JA. This is a last-resort scheduling measure where an airline forces the most junior legal flight attendant to work a flight during their scheduled day off or open time because all reserve crews have been exhausted. This prevents cancellations or other disruptions when the reserve pool runs out, and it typically falls on the most junior available flight attendant.

    This is used in cases such as major weather disruptions, holiday travel spikes, or high sick-call volume, after all on-call reserve flight attendants have already been assigned. Airlines assign these open trips starting from the absolute bottom of the seniority list at that base and working upward until the flight is covered. However, the fresh trip cannot violate mandatory rest requirements or maximum duty limits. This will also attract a premium payment, and the airline has to restore any lost days off.

    Industry observers note that contracts usually limit how often junior assignments can happen. PSA Airlines' contract caps it at three days a month and bars assignments that are more than 24 hours in advance, while Silver Airways' contract limits it to twice a month. They also usually pay at a premium rate of 150% at Silver Airways and PSA Airlines, and 2.5 times the trip rate under Alaska Airlines' 2025–2028 contract. Silver Airways closed down in June 2025.

    At some airlines, flight attendants who are already on duty at the airport, such as those arriving, checking in, or waiting in between flights, can be drafted onto another flight when time is critical, or the reserve pool is empty. Therefore, their entire schedule can change if a newly introduced trip is added or removed. Usually, crew scheduling tries not to disrupt the schedule too much and swaps them with a trip with similar timing, but of course, this is not always possible.

    Industry observers note that flight attendants on reserve or standby are usually more junior crew with low seniority, are on call, and can be given trips with little notice. Many US-based crew start out on reserve and may do so for the first few years. At American Airlines, for example, flight attendants are on reserve for the first year and then move to one month on reserve, one month off reserve until year five, when it moves to one month on reserve and three months off according to their APFA contract.

    It has been revealed that at Delta Air Lines, junior flight attendants bid on a line and do not have to complete a full month on reserve. Instead, they have six 'A' days a month, where they are on call. If a Delta flight attendant's trip is canceled or removed, they only keep their pay if they convert to availability. Delta's order of assignment places displaced lineholders on availability ahead of A-Day reserves, and management holds broader discretion to modify trips during irregular operations.

    It has been revealed that airlines in the rest of the world rarely have union agreements, and schedules are set by the operations or crew scheduling department. Rosters are scheduled four to six weeks in advance in accordance with duty time regulations, so you know what your trips will be and your days off, if all goes to plan. Long-haul rosters don't change much, but short-haul rosters are more likely to change. There is no bidding for trips, although crew can sometimes request one or two trips a month; it is rare that they are given. Part-time work is very rare.

    In addition, every crew member has some standby days, usually three or four per month, when you are on call to cover a trip at short notice because a flight attendant calls in sick or misses a trip. These are periods of around six to eight hours, and you would hope to be called at the beginning, not the end, of the shift. This can be at base, at the airport, or home standby; it varies by airline. Standby isn't just given to junior cabin crew; everyone has to do it, although seniority remains important throughout your career.

    Some airlines also have available days that are filled 12 to 24 hours in advance; you could get a trip, standby duty, or be stood down, and then it becomes a day off. If a change is made to your schedule by operations, it shows up on your roster, and that's it; you do the trip. There is no payment protection pay, sit pay, or any extra payments for schedule changes. Rosters are more likely to change at the last minute due to being called out on standby duty or if a flight is delayed and doesn't allow enough rest, but it is more likely on a short-haul or mixed-fleet roster.

    Every contract is different, so the rules, limits, and premium pay vary widely by airline and by where you are working. Large international airlines in Europe and the UK are not heavily unionized like those in the US, and they have no influence on your schedule or what you actually earn; that is up to the airline itself. In the Middle East, there are no unions.

    The contracts noted here are for comparison to show how contracts have changed in recent years and are for reference only; not all the airlines still exist, and some may have merged. American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Southwest Airlines contracts have all changed significantly in recent years, affecting how flight attendants are scheduled and paid. Delta's flight attendants are not unionized, so their scheduling rules come from organization policy rather than a contract.

    Recent findings suggest that terminology used by airlines can also be different. In the UK, Europe, and the Middle East, instead of reserve, we have standby, and instead of operating experience for junior flight attendants, we have supernumerary flights. We do not have "junior assignment," "junior availability," "drafting," "reassignment," and "displacement," which can all mean slightly different things depending on the contract. Although it's the same job with the same rules, the terminology, scheduling system, and pay are very different.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, president Trump has revived a claim that his private pilot previously relied on another country's air traffic control (ATC) system while flying in the US, prompting a public rebuttal from a private pilot. Speaking during a White House press conference on Friday, Trump criticized America's aviation infrastructure while discussing recent disruptions affecting the country's airspace, according to National Public Radio (NPR).

    In a recent development, the comments came one week after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of flights and just days after the administration requested another $50.1 billion for aviation modernization. However, Trump's account of using foreign controllers has raised questions about whether he meant air traffic control or the navigation technology installed aboard his aircraft.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the Daily Beast, Trump made the remarks during a "bonkers appearance" at a White House press conference addressing recent disruptions involving aviation, banking and communications networks. Asked about the incidents, the president maintained that they were unrelated, before discussing his personal experiences with private aviation.

    Trump described US ATC infrastructure as "ancient", and mentioned that his pilot had used foreign air traffic control before he entered office.

    “It's ancient! In fact, you know, before I was here, I had a plane. I had a very nice life. And my pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country. This was years ago, before I was in office. I don't want to say the country, but he found one country better than ours.”.

    The assertion prompted a response from journalist Brian Karem, who identified himself as a private pilot. In a post on X, Karem disputed the suggestion that pilots operating in US airspace could bypass domestic controllers by seeking assistance from another country. His objection centered on the distinction between the authorities controlling airspace and the equipment pilots use to navigate.

    "You cannot call up ATC in Europe and say, 'Hey give me a hand. I'm flying over US airspace.'".

    Trump's remarks were not entirely new. During the National Prayer Breakfast in February last year, he similarly claimed to use equipment or services from another country when landing his private aircraft in New York, according to Anadolu Ajansı. The comments attracted scrutiny from aviation experts at the time, Forbes reported.

    In a recent development, president Trump likely confused air traffic control systems with onboard navigation technology, according to Forbes. Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox explained that pilots operating under ATC supervision must comply with the applicable rules of that country, regardless of their navigation equipment's country of origin.

    It has been revealed that air traffic control and aircraft navigation perform very different functions. Controllers issue clearances, instructions and traffic information, while onboard navigation systems help pilots determine their position and follow flight looks. An aircraft operating under instrument flight rules in controlled US airspace cannot simply select a foreign ATC provider. The differences are summarized below:.

    Provides clearances, traffic separation and instructions.

    Provides satellite-based positioning and navigation.

    Calculates and manages the aircraft's flight path.

    Inertial reference system (IRS).

    Tracks aircraft position and movement using onboard sensors.

    Provide route, waypoint and procedure information.

    Provide navigation, communication or flight management capabilities.

    Sources indicate that A plausible explanation is that Trump's aircraft used internationally manufactured avionics, navigation databases, or satellite-based positioning technology. As the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual explains, these technologies provide navigation guidance but do not replace ATC services. Without confirmation from Trump's former pilots, the precise technology he was describing remains unknown.

    Recent findings suggest that the dispute comes amid growing pressure to modernize the FAA's aging infrastructure. On November 13, a telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop lasting nearly five hours. According to the FAA's subsequent investigation, excessive network traffic destabilized legacy equipment, affecting communications and radar feeds at 17 of the country's 22 enroute control centers. Approximately 12,500 flights were canceled that day, and hundreds more over the days that followed.

    On November 17, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and Budget Director Russell Vought formally requested $50.1 billion from Congress. The proposal follows $12.5 billion approved in July 2025 and would finance technology upgrades, replacement facilities, and airport infrastructure. The administration's request is broken down as follows:.

    ATC technology and digital modernization.

    Airport infrastructure improvements.

    Five consolidated enroute control centers.

    Construction and upgrades of up to 140 ATC towers.

    It has been revealed that the FAA aims to complete the first phase of its Brand New Air Traffic Control System by December 2028. However, in September, the Government Accountability Office warned that incomplete cost estimates and scheduling would undermine progress. Although the need for modernization is well documented, it does not establish that foreign controllers previously managed Trump's flights within US airspace. The president's renewed remarks therefore leave the original technical question unresolved.
