    #30985. Breaking: Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1355 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine.
    • The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B.
    • In a recent development, for airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine. However, each of these aircraft uses a different variation of that same turbofan that is tailored to its unique needs and engineering qualities.

    The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B. Boeing chose the GEnx for the 747-8 primarily to modernize the aging jumbo jet with next-generation technology. Both aircraft feature distinctive serrated chevrons on the engine nacelles, which mix hot exhaust with cool air to significantly reduce noise.

    In a recent development, for airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training. The GEnx-1B is a larger, more powerful, and more-electric engine designed for a modern twin-engine jet. The GEnx-2B is a smaller, simplified variant that incorporates traditional pneumatics to breathe life into the older 747 systems while providing modern fuel efficiency.

    Industry observers note that while the GEnx-1B (787) and GEnx-2B (747-8) share a common high-pressure core and 80% of their Line Replaceable Units, they are distinct engines optimized for different aircraft architectures. The most fundamental difference is how the engines interact with the aircraft's internal systems. The GEnx family is designed to stay on wing 20% longer than previous generations, with some fleet leaders exceeding 30,000 hours without a major overhaul.

    Sources indicate that both engines offer approximately 15% better fuel efficiency than the older CF6 engines they replaced. Tom Levin, General Manager of the GEnx/CF6 engine product line at GE Aviation, commented on the engine's success when the 1,000th GEnx engine was developed in 2015.

    Recent findings suggest that “The GEnx was the fastest selling engine in GE’s history, and now it is the fastest production ramp up of a GE widebody engine program. The GEnx engine has proven itself with outstanding performance and reliability.".

    The 787 uses a bleedless architecture where most systems are powered electrically. The 747-8 uses a traditional bleed-air system to power environmental controls and start the engines, requiring the GEnx-2B to include bleed-air ports. The GEnx-2B has fewer stages in the booster and low-pressure turbine, optimizing it for a four-engine configuration.

    It has been revealed that the Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, uses a traditional bleed air system. It must bleed high-pressure air from the compressor to power the 747’s pneumatic systems, including cabin pressurization and thermal anti-icing.

    According to recent reports, to fit the 747’s wing and ground clearance, the GEnx-2B has a smaller fan diameter, 105 inches, compared to the 787’s 111 inches. Because the 747-8 has four engines while the 787 has only two, the -2B is simplified internally to be lighter and more optimized for its lower per-engine thrust requirement. The -2B produces roughly 66,500 lbs of thrust, whereas the 787 variants can reach up to 76,100 lbs.

    Recent findings suggest that the GEnx-1B has more power because it is intended for a twin-engine aircraft (787) that must maintain performance in the event of an engine failure during takeoff. Because the GEnx-2B's power is distributed across four engines on the 747-8, its thrust rating is 66,500 lbf lower. Compared with older engines like the CF6, the GEnx-2B's technology improves fuel efficiency and cuts emissions by 15%.

    Sources indicate that in contrast to the 1B, the GEnx-2B has de-staged components to maximize weight and performance for a four-engine setup. In contrast to the 1B's four stages, the 2B's low-pressure compressor has three stages. In the low-pressure turbine, the 1B has seven stages, whereas the 2B has six.

    Compared with the 747-8, the 787 Dreamliner delivers bettereconomics and is much more efficient in the widebody market, as it is a lightweight twin-engine composite aircraft. These engineering variations determine their efficiency and commercial success. The 747 uses about 3,800 gallons of fuel per hour, while the 787 uses about 2,900 gallons. The 787-9 is extremely efficient, using approximately 2.31 liters per 100 km per passenger, which is significantly better than the 747-8's 2.82 liters per 100 km per passenger.

    According to recent reports, boeing's Dreamliner also costs significantly less to operate, with a lower cost per available seat mile. Airlines typically prefer smaller twin-engine aircraft because they are less dangerous to fill and fly. The 787's design and performance have allowed it to thrive in the modern aviation market, while the 747-8 saw limited passenger orders before production ended in 2017 and the 747 assembly line fully shut down in 2023.

    The Dreamliner has essentially eliminated the conventional hub-and-spoke paradigm that made the 747 necessary. While the 747 required high passenger capacity to be successful, the 787's efficiency lets it cover the same distances with fewer seats, making it a better match for today's point-to-point market.

    The 787's efficiency allows airlines to launch new, nonstop point-to-point routes that would not have been economically viable with older, bigger, four-engine planes. Despite being more efficient than previous 747s, the 747-8 is still best suited to high-volume hub-to-hub services. Airlines such as United have made large 787 orders to replace a mix of 747s, 767s, and early 777s with a single, simpler aircraft family, resulting in significant cost savings for pilot training and component inventory.

    Industry observers note that the 787 incorporates a large amount of carbon composite material, making it lighter, more resistant to fatigue and corrosion, and allowing for higher cabin humidity and lower cabin altitude, which enhances passenger comfort and reduces structural stress. The 747-8 is a development of a traditional aluminum design, with a heavier base structure.

    Sources indicate that lufthansa has incorporated the 787-9 to handle flights that need the same range but have about 70–90 fewer people, even though it is still a 747-8 operator. Because of this, even at off-peak times, the airline can maintain high load factors (percentage of seats filled). British Airways switched to the 787-10 for notable transatlantic flights to New York and Chicago after retiring its entire 747 fleet. The 787-10 is 25% more fuel-efficient than the 747 while offering comparable cargo capacity and contemporary comforts.

    Compared to the 747, the 787 Dreamliner offers a better long-haul passenger experience because its composite airframe creates a cabin environment that more closely resembles ground conditions. When compared to older aircraft like the 747, which have a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet, the 787's cabin altitude of 6,000 feet makes a significant difference for passengers. That lower cabin altitude does many things to reduce the effects of fatigue on passengers inflight.

    Industry observers note that the composite construction of the 787 is not only 50% by weight but 80% by volume. Thanks to that light yet incredibly durable construction, it can do things no previous aircraft could. That includes having larger windows, higher humidity (15% or double that of legacy jets), and a more spacious interior with more natural lighting and better overhead storage.

    Industry observers note that while the 747 is much loved for its incredibly smooth landing characteristics and gentle handling and flight, the 787 uses a fresh technology known as 'smooth ride' to counteract turbulence in flight. This is the same technology that the 777X will use when it finally debuts in 2027. Although the 747 was known as the Queen of the Skies, the Dreamliner has become the best-selling widebody in history. It has been the flagship product of the legendary plane maker, as its 737 MAX has flailed in the wake of a disastrous debut.

    This is not only a major improvement for the long-haul market, but also for operators that use these aircraft for high-density hub-to-hub transport, and makes a major improvement for the densest routes in the world. A 787 Dreamliner is not only a game-changer for the operators that fly it, but it also marks a paradigm shift in the experience for flyers. While the era of the 747 ushered in a golden age of jet-powered commercial aviation, the 787 and future successors such as the 777X herald the next era in air travel.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….
    • With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.
    • We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    According to recent reports, here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    Sources indicate that after that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it indicates this:.

    Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    Industry observers note that it’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary notes something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet right now consists of 25 planes, including:.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet right now consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was declared by the organization’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    The proposal is for the 787-9s to get all-upcoming cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

    According to recent reports, the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

    We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s fresh premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s upcoming Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    Recent findings suggest that aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's fresh premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the newly introduced Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

    Sources indicate that aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

    #30980. Why Are All Pratt & Whitney's GTF Engines Green On The Inside?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1609 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Are All Pratt & Whitney's GTF Engines Green On The Inside?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Passengers boarding an Airbus A320neo or an A220 who glance at the engine intake from the jet bridge often notice something unusual.
    • The more convincing answers sit in materials science and maintenance practice.
    • The broad green band lining the inner surface of the fan case is the engine’s acoustic liner, a panel built from a perforated skin bonded over a honeycomb core.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Passengers boarding an Airbus A320neo or an A220 who glance at the engine intake from the jet bridge often notice something unusual. Inside the nacelle, ahead of the fan blades, a ring of teal green lines the casing of the Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan, whether the aircraft carries the PW1100G of the A320neo family or the PW1500G of the A220. The color is consistent enough across the fleet that spotters and online aviation communities have debated its purpose for years, with explanations ranging from branding to corrosion protection.

    The more convincing answers sit in materials science and maintenance practice. Two separate components contribute to the green appearance, each with its own function and its own reason for the shade it carries, and a third factor, the practical needs of the people who inspect the engines, explains why the color has persisted. Examining those components in turn clarifies how a modern geared turbofan manages noise, tip clearance, and inspection, and why a seemingly cosmetic detail reflects engineering decisions made well before the engine reaches an airline.

    The broad green band lining the inner surface of the fan case is the engine’s acoustic liner, a panel built from a perforated skin bonded over a honeycomb core. The perforations admit sound waves into the cells of the honeycomb, where each cell behaves like a small resonant chamber that absorbs acoustic energy and converts a portion of it into heat. By sizing the cells and the perforated face sheet for particular frequencies, designers tune the panel to dampen the tones that dominate fan noise.

    Industry observers note that the geared architecture makes this component especially relevant. Because a reduction gearbox lets the fan turn more slowly than the turbine driving it, the engine produces a different acoustic signature from a direct-drive fan of similar size, with more of the energy at lower frequencies. Low-frequency sound is harder to absorb than high-frequency sound, since longer wavelengths need deeper cavities to dissipate effectively, which is why the liner occupies a generous stretch of the inlet. Pratt & Whitney has promoted the engine’s reduced noise footprint as a headline benefit, and the liner is one of several features that contribute to it alongside the slower fan itself.

    Sources indicate that construction follows a sandwich principle common to aerospace structures. A solid backing sheet closes one side of the honeycomb, and the perforated face sheet closes the other. The arrangement delivers acoustic performance with very little weight, a priority in any component carried on an engine hanging from the wing, where added mass raises fuel burn. The panels are also designed to withstand airflow, vibration, temperature swings, and minor debris impacts throughout a long service life.

    The teal shade is generally attributed to the composite itself rather than to a decorative coating. According to descriptions of the construction, the resin and epoxy matrix that bind the liner’s layers carry a natural pigmentation that indicates through on the finished surface. Engineers have a practical reason to avoid covering it. A thick film of paint would partially fill the microscopic perforations in the face sheet, reducing the open area through which sound enters the cavities and degrading the attenuation the panel was designed to achieve.

    However, this explanation should be treated with some caution, because there has not been a published manufacturer statement regarding the color. As a result, the exact origin of the hue remains an informed inference rather than a documented fact. The uniform result across A320neo and A220 installations nonetheless suggests a controlled material choice instead of an incidental one.

    Directly aft of the acoustic ring sits a slightly lighter blue-green band, the abradable rub strip, which technical literature also calls a fan outer air seal. Its job is to control the gap between the fan blade tips and the surrounding case. Any air that leaks across that gap represents lost work, so engine makers want the clearance as small as practical without allowing the blades to strike a hard surface.

    The abradable material solves that problem by being softer than the blade tips. During break-in, the tips cut a shallow groove into the strip, producing a seal matched to the actual shape of that particular fan, including any slight growth caused by heat and centrifugal loading. The strip wears while the blades and the case remain intact. A paper from the 2003 NASA Seal/Secondary Air System Workshop, which covers Pratt & Whitney abradable seals, documents the broader engineering approach behind such materials.

    The color of this strip carries its own explanation. The compound is supplied as a two-part epoxy and hardener, and the components are mixed to a defined turquoise shade so that a uniform color confirms the two parts were blended properly before application. Streaks or patches of a different tone would signal incomplete mixing, and with it a risk that the cured strip will not abrade predictably. The compound’s behavior over time matters as much as its initial performance. As the engine accumulates cycles, the strip gradually erodes from airflow, particles, and repeated light contact, and clearance grows accordingly. Operators therefore monitor the condition of the strip during scheduled inspections and restore it when wear exceeds published limits, a process that depends on repeating the same mixing and curing steps, and the same color check, each time the material is applied.

    Sources indicate that beyond material chemistry, the saturated green interior gives maintenance crews a practical advantage during walk-around checks. The fan case sits in a shadowed cavity, and the blades, the hub, and any dark residue around the casing can blend together in poor light. A bright, uniform background makes departures from normal appearance easier to see.

    Ramp inspectors look for several conditions in this region. Foreign object debris, such as fragments of tire, packing material, or bird remains, stands out against the green surface. Erosion of the liner or the rub strip shows as lighter patches or exposed honeycomb, and abnormal wear on the blade tips appears as unusual rub patterns where the strip has been cut. Because these checks often occur between flights under airport lighting and on tight schedules, a background that makes anomalies obvious reduces the chance of a missed finding.

    The choice of green also reflects how the human eye distinguishes color. Green sits near the middle of the visible spectrum, where daylight vision is most sensitive, and it contrasts strongly with the reds, browns, and oranges typical of oil, hydraulic fluid, and corrosion products, so a stain or deposit on the liner is easier to notice than it would be on a gray or white surface.

    The GTF is far from the first aircraft component to appear in this color. Aerospace suppliers have long finished parts in green, and BMT Aerospace notes that the shade is often traced to protective primers applied to metal surfaces to resist corrosion. Zinc chromate primer, widely used for decades on airframes and components, has a distinctive yellow-green tone, which is why green surfaces are a familiar sight inside wheel wells, wing bays, and equipment racks.

    Public discussion has also linked the GTF’s green interior to Pratt & Whitney’s environmental positioning, since the engine is marketed on lower fuel burn, reduced emissions, and quieter operation. This reading is plausible as a secondary benefit but lacks documentary support, and the engineering explanations above are sufficient on their own. A color that doubles as a reminder of the engine’s efficiency claims costs the manufacturer nothing, which may be why no one has felt a need to change it.

    The green interior of the GTF is a small example of a larger trend in which material properties are doing more of the work that markings once did. As engines move toward larger, slower fans housed in shorter nacelles, liners will have to absorb more sound from less surface area, which pushes designers toward more sophisticated core geometries and multilayer constructions. Pratt & Whitney’s improved GTF Advantage variant retains the same gearbox architecture, so the existing liner conventions should carry forward into the newer engines.

    Recent findings suggest that inspection practice is also changing. Airlines and maintenance providers are adopting borescope automation, drone-assisted visual checks, and machine-vision software that compares images against a reference baseline. A controlled, repeatable color simplifies that comparison, because software can flag deviations in hue or texture more reliably when the underlying surface is uniform. Should manufacturers publish color tolerances for liners and rub strips, the green interior could evolve from an informal convention into a formal measurement reference, with deviations scored automatically before a technician reaches the engine.

    In a recent development, material choices will also respond to environmental scrutiny. Chromate-based primers are under regulatory pressure in several jurisdictions because of worker exposure and disposal concerns, and the industry is moving toward alternatives. Any substitute for current coatings will need to preserve acoustic openness, bonding strength, and the visual contrast that crews rely on, which may lead suppliers to add deliberate pigments where natural color once sufficed.

    According to recent reports, for the existing fleet, the near-term picture is straightforward. With a large and growing fleet in service, the teal ring is likely to remain a recognizable feature for decades, and its meaning will rest on data as much as on appearance. Operators who record inspection images consistently over an engine’s life will build a visual history of wear that could support condition-based maintenance, replacing fixed intervals with decisions informed by measured trends in clearance and liner condition. In that sense, the color’s greatest value may lie ahead of it, as a standardized backdrop for the analytics that will govern how these engines are maintained.

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard.
    • Sources indicate that this system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service problems at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge.
    • Industry observers note that emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

    Sources indicate that this system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service problems at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a upcoming initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

    Industry observers note that emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

    Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a fresh initiative involving this small group of employees:.

    On 3 November, Emirates introduced a newly introduced initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

    This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

    So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

    A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

    Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

    For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

    It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

    As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

    According to recent reports, I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

    Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

    In a recent development, emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

    There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

    What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

    It has been revealed that I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager.     Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus fresh ways that housing rewards are offered.

    There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a upcoming month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal).     There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

    Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

    Sources indicate that bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

    Sources indicate that on the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

    For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

    Sources indicate that on December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:.

    Industry observers note that let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

    On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:.

    The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:.

    Recent findings suggest that regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

    This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

    Sources indicate that on the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

    One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

    Latest Update: Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I promptly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I promptly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    It has been revealed that I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    It has been revealed that I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    It has been revealed that as the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically noted, “that means nothing.”.

    So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    Sources indicate that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Sources indicate that back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That stated, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    In a recent development, inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    Recent findings suggest that the legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    In a recent development, imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of latest Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    In a recent development, if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    Hi Daniel! Great review but I’m afraid I might have to disagree a little with you here based on my personal experiences with AR this April and November. It is a shame that FB sent you an email that conflicted with AR’s policy. I suspect that it might be FB’s fault and not AR because it’s a standard email template. I flew with AR 4 times this year both domestically within Argentina and internationally. Their unconventional luggage allowance was stated quite clearly at online check-in. Unless you did not check in online or missed it ;). As for the checked luggage allowance in practice, I’ve found that it’s a YMMV situation. On 3 of my 4 legs with AR this year, the check-in agents accepted all the bags that I had paid for and the cabin bags that I had not. On my fourth leg AEP-IGR about two weeks ago (early Nov 2026), the agent told me that I had exceeded my allowance by one entire piece that weighed 8kg, which was unfortunate but fair. I had to pay the fee outside and it came up to US$10. Unlike you however, I did not have to go back in to show my EMD as proof of payment. It was automatically dispatched. I had some time at AEP and a chatty agent with whom I could practice my imperfect Argentine Spanish. She clarified with a few shrugs that there is no clear formula for calculating the fee. It seems to be a combination of fare class, date of booking mixed in with some Argentine chaos and charm. The maintenance issues, delays and their handling of irregular ops are two other stories altogether though.

    Glad to always hear more about AR, even if it is not always positive news, and welcome to the blog ^^.

    @Daniel - You mentioned in this post that GRU doesn't have a priority fast track lane. I flew out of there this past August (on AA, I believe it was Terminal 3, but I may be wrong). That terminal did have a priority lane which I believe was for Visa Infinite cardmembers issued in Brazil (or may have been for Amex Platinum cardmembers - I have both so can't remember). All I remember is seeing the entrance, going up to ask if I could use it, and was told it's only for people with cards issued in Brazil.

    I flew Lufthansa recently and had the same feeling about it as you did about Aerolineas - a flag carrier masquerading as a full-service airline. At the gates, at least for intra-Europe segments, they're out aggressively pulling passengers aside to fit their hand luggage into a sizer and when the bag fails to fit, charging €110 to check it. The hand luggage allotment seems designed specifically to rope passengers into this fee, given the sizing relative to what appeared to me to be very generously-sized overhead bins on board compared with what is standard in America. What floors me the most is that there is apparently a weight limit on carry-on luggage of 8 kg - my personal item probably exceeds that weight, much less a suitcase. I've no idea why it should matter whether I'm flying with cinder blocks as long as my bag fits in the sizer. On board, everything is buy on board outside of a small, quarter liter bottle of water. I know that airlines like Lufthansa feel that they have to use this type of model in order to compete with the likes of Ryanair, but at least Ryanair is honest about what it is rather than trying to portray itself as some sort of bespoke, luxury experience.

    Took the same trip myself earlier this year. I always make a point of checking baggage allowances with carrier airlines. I would note that the majority of airlines do an incredibly poor job of detailing exactly what benefits (or not) you get on the airlines they partner with. I actually wasn't that surprised by the flight. It was clean, reasonably comfortable, and it's a v short flight. You're 100% accurate that the priority club lounge has a surprisingly broad food and drink options, comfortable seating, and also when we were there mid-morning, completely empty apart from us.

    #30975. Citi Shop offers an easier way to save when shopping online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1049 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    Citi Shop offers an easier way to save when shopping online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online.
    • Recent findings suggest that it has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants.
    • Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

    Recent findings suggest that it has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

    Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

    Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

    According to recent reports, citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

    Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

    Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

    Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

    In a recent development, but Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

    All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

    What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

    Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

    In a recent development, generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

    Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points.

    Industry observers note that unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

    According to recent reports, even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

    In a recent development, I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

    Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

    Industry observers note that if you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a major benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

    But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

    Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

    Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

    Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

    Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi states statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

    In a recent development, in many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT.".

    If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

    In a recent development, citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

    To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

    Related: The best credit cards for online shopping.

    #30974. FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 45m • 📚 Deep Dive (9041 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (9041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas.
    • There’s a real oversight question here.
    • It has been revealed that the November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas. Now the story is becoming about Elon Musk: a claim that DOGE cut FAA employees, oversight was loosened, and this led to the flight stoppage. There’s a real oversight question here. It long predates DOGE. In fact it goes back decades. And even there, the connection between specific oversight failures and what actually happened hasn’t been made. Anyone writing about this needs to at least know that an L3Harris contractor’s router configuration error caused a nationwide air traffic disruption in 2009, too. And federal investigators criticized the FAA’s oversight after that incident! FAA problems did not begin with DOGE. A Router Change Disrupted The National Network The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and lasted until 8:15 p.m. Aircraft already airborne continued landing. The FAA’s preliminary account describes excessive connection attempts flooding its telecommunications network. Instability affected 17 of 22 enroute centers and spread to approach facilities. L3Harris had installed a router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Investigators also identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Blocking those sites stabilized the network, and officials disabled the relevant function on more than 60 similar routers. FAA Oversight Has Been A Problem, Long Before DOGE One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford stated the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union unveiled that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . Elon Musk’s February 27, 2025 correction identifying L3Harris’s legacy network It’s hard to blame Musk when he was literally warning about failure of this specific network. And it shows the FAA was aware of risk that predated the current administration. Indeed, DOGE was aware of the risk, and its titular head shouted it from the rooftops. I was skeptical that DOGE would fix the FAA when Duffy first invited Musk’s team in. It was asking for a cat, provided it barked. Government agencies behave as they do because of their incentives. Their problems aren’t generally that nobody smart enough or sufficiently determined has shown up to fix them. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits! The FAA Has Spent Decades Failing To Deliver Promised Upgrades The FAA was testing replacements for paper flight strips in 1983. It’s still rolling them out. Canada completed its commercial airport and terminal facility rollout by 2006, according to the Eno Transportation Center’s history of the two countries’ efforts. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges users and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Proposal Air Traffic Systems And Facilities Airport Projects $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act $12.1 billion $18 billion $50.1 billion administration request $30.1 billion $20 billion The latest $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits! The FAA Has Spent Decades Failing To Deliver Promised Upgrades The FAA was testing replacements for paper flight strips in 1983. It’s still rolling them out. Canada completed its commercial airport and terminal facility rollout by 2006, according to the Eno Transportation Center’s history of the two countries’ efforts. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges people and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Proposal Air Traffic Systems And Facilities Airport Projects $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act $12.1 billion $18 billion $50.1 billion administration request $30.1 billion $20 billion The newly introduced $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions.     Industry observers note that one Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford said the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union unveiled that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). .     #30973. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class
